title: Novo Nordisk Q2 2026 Review: Better Than Feared But Is It Enough?
snippet: We were right about the trough, but the turnaround might be messier than expected...
content_html:
Exactly 6 months after our FY2025 review, Novo has already raised the guidance we called too conservative. The commercial thesis is improving faster than expected. The pipeline thesis is not.

For reference, here is our FY2025 Review & 2026 Outlook posted on February 7:

So, back in February, after Novo Nordisk published its FY2025 results and rather brutal 2026 guidance, we argued that the central question was whether 2026 represented a temporary reset in the economics of the business, or the beginning of a permanently lower-growth, lower-margin Novo Nordisk.

We also wrote that management’s original guidance for a 5% to 13% decline in adjusted sales and operating profit at constant exchange rates (CER) looked excessively conservative. We expected the year to be ugly, but suspected Novo was deliberately leaving itself plenty of room to “undepromise and overdeliver”.

Now, we finally have enough evidence to start marking that thesis. And the answer is rather interesting. We were right about several of the most important things. We were wrong, or at least too optimistic, about another one.

Let’s have a look into it!

Executive Overview

Novo’s Q2 was substantially better than the headline reaction would suggest.

Adjusted Q2 sales reached DKK 78.5B, growing 7% at CER, while adjusted operating profit increased 11% to DKK 33.4B. For H1, adjusted sales and operating profit both grew 2% at CER. Obesity care grew 16% in Q2, while International Operations grew 10%. Most importantly, Novo raised its full-year outlook again.

Let’s remember where we started…

In February, management guided to a -5% to -13% in adjusted sales and operating profit. After Q1, that became a -4% to -12%. Now it is 0% to -6%. The midpoint has therefore moved from roughly -9% to -3% in 6 months.

That is a fairly significant change to the earnings trajectory we were supposed to be terrified of back in February. Yet Novo’s US-listed shares fell roughly 6% after the results. Investors focused on Wegovy pill sales of about DKK 3.2B coming slightly below expectations, the latest CagriSema data, continued pricing pressure and growing concern around the pipeline.

One important conclusion from first half of 2026:

The commercial turnaround is becoming visible. The R&D turnaround, however, is not.

1. The Quarter Was Better Than It Looks

Novo’s reported H1 numbers are almost useless without adjustment. Reported H1 sales grew 18% at CER and operating profit grew 27%, but those numbers contain the DKK 26.8B reversal of a US 340B rebate provision recorded in Q1. The reversal had no cash impact. On an adjusted basis, H1 sales and operating profit both grew only 2%.

Q2 subsequently gave us a cleaner picture. Adjusted sales grew 7%, driven primarily by GLP-1 volumes, while adjusted operating profit grew faster at 11%. Obesity care sales increased 16%, with International Operations obesity sales up 37%. US adjusted sales returned to 4% growth after falling 11% at CER in Q1.

These numbers are important because our February thesis didn’t require Novo to suddenly become a 20% grower again. We explicitly argued that the stock could work simply on “down less than expected” and improving visibility, before the income statement looked beautiful.

And that is actually almost exactly what has happened. The original 2026 guidance was too conservative and we got that right. But there is an important ‘but’. Novo’s new full-year guidance still calls for flat to -6% growth despite Q2 growing 7%. Management is thus clearly expecting a tougher second half as pricing, competition and other headwinds continue to work through the P&L.

So this quarter doesn’t really show the crisis is over, it’s just less severe than management feared (or, deliberately presented). And that might not be quite enough for the turnaround story to, you know, start turning around…

2. "Volume Up, Price Down" Is Actually Working

One of the central stress tests in our February article was whether Novo could survive a period in which prices fell while patient volumes continued expanding and the bear case was quite straightforward here - demand could look fantastic while the economics quietly deteriorated underneath it. And that risk hasn’t really disappeared.

US H1 adjusted sales were still -4% at CER, and Novo continues to explicitly cite lower realised prices. Even in Q2, the return to 4% US growth benefited from favourable rebate adjustments.

But the other half of our thesis for FY2026 is also materialising. International Operations grew 10% in Q2, obesity sales outside the US grew 37% and EUCAN grew 17% overall. Novo now reaches 4.9 million obesity patients, compared with 2.9 million a year earlier.

We wrote in February that the bull case could survive if international growth and mix could absorb some of the US compression, and we can see that happening in real time. Not completely and not yet sufficiently enough to restore the old growth profile but quite enough for Novo’s global infrastructure to actually matter.

3. Wegovy Pill Is More Important Than DKK 3.2B

This might be the most important part of Q2.

Wegovy pill generated DKK 3.22B ($500 million) of adjusted Q2 sales and more than 5 million US prescriptions since launch. Weekly prescriptions exceeded 265,000 by 17 July, making it the strongest GLP-1 volume launch Novo has recorded. Around 30% of prescriptions have already progressed to the 9 mg and 25 mg doses.

Wall Street was (again… or, still?) disappointed because pill sales came slightly below consensus. Read that again and try not to get furious. :)

From our point of view, this is also truly a sign of the times, as far as sentiment about the company goes. You can have literally one of the strongest pharmaceutical launches by volume in history, obliterate competition’s counterpart (Lilly’s Foundayo) and somehow still end up being a disappointment and just not enough? And then proceed to tank up to -10% on a random unimportant failed trail, which is quite literally a side-quest for the company, nothing-burger type of news? It’s rather ridiculous how this keeps going on - groundbreaking positive news get +2% (and back to break-even in after hours) and nothing-news with slightly negative connotation get -5% to -10% on the day. As we said, a sign of the times…

Okay, rant time over, let’s talk about how we’re much more interested in who is actually entering the market because the pill exists.

In February we argued that obesity treatment would stratify across injections, pills, reimbursed access, self-pay and different price points, and that Novo didn’t need to beat Lilly everywhere. It needed enough products to capture different patient cohorts.

And the first international launch offers fascinating evidence. Novo’s UK presentation estimates roughly 300,000 patients adopted Wegovy pill within the first 3 weeks. What’s more, the total obesity market expanded sharply after launch rather than showing a simple 1-for-1 transfer from injections. Novo’s estimated market share also increased from roughly 30% to 45%. However, these data are preliminary and extrapolated from a concentrated private market, so don’t take the precise percentages too seriously. The direction and dynamics are still clear, though.

The pill may be creating patients, not just “stealing” them.

That is vastly more valuable than arguing over whether quarterly sales missed consensus by measly DKK 100M.

There is another underappreciated detail. Medicare Part D access through Novo’s Bridge programme only began on 1 July, after Q2 ended. Q2 sales therefore barely contain the benefit of this additional access channel.

And Novo has something else it can monetise as well - semaglutide’s maturity. The company highlights a US oral label combining 16.6% mean weight loss, a 20% reduction in major cardiovascular events derived from the semaglutide evidence base, around 50 million patient-years of real-world exposure and fewer drug interaction restrictions than Lilly’s oral competitor.

The comparison comes from Novo itself and should be treated accordingly, but this is exactly the kind of differentiation that can matter to physicians and payers once oral obesity therapy becomes crowded.

Efficacy gets the headline and impulse upwards stock movement but evidence, familiarity, access and prescribing simplicity can get the actual prescription and long-term winning chances.

4. 78.2% Gross Margin Needs an Asterisk

At first glance, this is where our February thesis appears to be going wrong. Novo’s gross margin was 81.0% for FY2025. Q1 2026 adjusted gross margin was 80.6%. Q2 fell to just 78.2%. Clearly no bueno. We specifically said we wanted to see gross margin stop stepping down.

So, fail? Not quite.

Novo disclosed that Q2 contained approximately DKK 3B of one-time costs from right-sizing manufacturing capacity agreements, alongside lower realised prices and negative currency effects. Productivity gains and favourable GLP-1 mix partially offset those pressures.

When we mechanically add that DKK 3B back to Q2 gross profit, we get a margin of roughly 82%.

That isn’t a company-adjusted metric and we shouldn’t pretend the pricing pressure is disappearing but it completely changes how one should interpret the headline figure of 78.2%. The quarter doesn’t demonstrate that Novo’s underlying gross margin suddenly collapsed by 450 basis points.

There is also evidence that the 2025 restructuring is producing real savings. Sales and distribution costs fell 13% at CER in Q2 while Novo was simultaneously funding the Wegovy pill and high-dose launches. Adjusted operating margin remained an extraordinary 42.5%.

Our updated judgement on margins is therefore not red but it’s not really green, either. The one-time manufacturing charge means the headline number exaggerates deterioration, but lower realised pricing remains very real. We need another couple of quarters before objectively claiming the economics have stabilised (or has truly deteriorated).

5. A Tiny Detail From Canada

Buried in the geographic commentary is perhaps the best live experiment Novo investors have for the eventual semaglutide patent cliff.

Novo says that loss of exclusivity for semaglutide in Canada has already resulted in lower realised prices, while its volumes have remained broadly stable. We see Canada becoming a small, imperfect preview of what happens when semaglutide loses exclusivity.

So far, the result of this is clearly “the economics compress”.

Obviously Canada is not the United States, and one quarter tells us very little about the eventual 2030s landscape. But investors should follow this closely because it helps separate two very different patent-cliff risks. One is franchise destruction and the other one is margin compression around a franchise that retains enormous volume.

Those produce two very different terminal values and stock prices. Nevertheless, we would sleep better if our thesis plays out before 2032, ideally before 2031, and this the a big reason why. :)

6. Where Our Thesis Has Gotten Worse: The Pipeline

If the commercial side deserves an upgrade, the metabolic pipeline deserves a downgrade.

Share Hated Moats

This was one of our February conditions: pipeline and lifecycle milestones had to remain credible, because Novo eventually needs to bridge beyond semaglutide.

Since then, CagriSema has repeatedly failed to establish the clean differentiation investors wanted. In the newly completed REIMAGINE 4 diabetes trial, CagriSema was non-inferior to tirzepatide on weight loss, with 15.2% versus 15.8%, but failed non-inferiority on HbA1c reduction, at 1.9 percentage points versus 2.2 points.

CagriSema is still a very effective medicine. Its obesity programme has produced compelling absolute weight loss and an FDA decision remains expected in Q4. But “very effective” and “strategically re-differentiating Novo from Lilly” aren’t the same statement.

At the same time, Novo booked DKK 6.3B of Q2 pipeline impairments, including DKK 4B related to terminated monlunabant. Ziltivekimab subsequently failed the ZEUS cardiovascular outcomes trial with a hazard ratio of 0.99, essentially no benefit on the primary MACE endpoint, while serious infections were more frequent.

Tragedy? Well, the whole pipeline isn’t failing. Etavopivat, for example, successfully met both primary endpoints in Phase 3 sickle-cell disease. But for the question investors care about most, what replaces or extends the semaglutide empire, Q2 didn’t make us more comfortable. And to be perfectly honest, this is yet another reason why we’d prefer to be out of the stock by 2031.

So, this is where our February bull case has weakened. Management appears to recognise it. Novo is increasingly presenting partnerships and acquisitions as a core component of R&D, and CEO Mike Doustdar has explicitly talked about accelerating development and pursuing bolt-on deals, and that can work. It just simply means part of Novo’s future moat may need to be purchased rather than invented internally.

7. Novo Versus Lilly: We Still Think People Are Asking the Wrong Question

just produced another monster quarter. Mounjaro generated almost $10B and Zepbound nearly $5B in Q2, reinforcing its clear leadership in injectable momentum.

Pretending is currently “winning” the overall GLP-1 race would be silly.

But our February argument looks even more relevant today, and it’s something we’ve been saying for almost a year now. Novo doesn’t need to beat Lilly everywhere. Lilly is winning the injectable growth race. But Novo is currently winning the oral obesity launch.

There can be two enormous franchises inside a market where only around 1% of the world’s population with obesity is currently treated with branded anti-obesity medicines. The more important question is whether Novo can preserve acceptable economics while serving that market.

And that one remains unanswered for now.

So, Were We Right?

On the biggest near-term call, yes.

The original 2026 guidance was too conservative. The earnings trough is proving shallower than management initially suggested. International obesity growth is helping offset US pressure and oral Wegovy is demonstrating that different delivery formats can expand the market rather than merely cannibalise it. Access is improving and cost reductions are appearing.

On pricing, the answer is incomplete. Realised prices are still falling, but volume is increasingly offsetting the damage.

On margins, the raw 78.2% figure looks frightening, but the DKK 3B manufacturing charge means it cannot be extrapolated. We have early evidence of stabilisation, but not rock-solid proof.

On pipeline credibility, however, things are worse than we wanted or would like to see. CagriSema hasn’t established clear superiority over tirzepatide, monlunabant is gone and ZEUS failed.

And the other warning from February has also survived. Novo continues to generate an absurd number of adjustments, provision reversals, impairments, rebate timing effects and restructuring-related items. We specifically listed “repeated one-offs that keep muddying the base business” as something to watch. Well, they’re still muddying it, and we’re still not happy about it…

What we are happy about, though, is clear change in approach to PR - more bold presentation and demeanour, better marketing, not highlighting negatives in the style of “oh poor us, at least we’re honest” pseudo-humble way but confidently pushing positives instead, suing Lilly for fake claims in marketing, etc… Novo really needed that!

Conclusion

6 months ago we described 2026 as potentially the painful trough through which the market was extrapolating permanent damage. We believe that Q2 (or the whole H1 2026 for that matter) makes that interpretation more credible.

Novo’s commercial moat hasn’t disappeared. More than 5 million Wegovy pill prescriptions, rapid international expansion, improving access, extraordinarily high patient demand and a manufacturing network capable of supplying multiple formulations don’t look like the fingerprints of a broken franchise.

At the same time, while expanding to the world (UAE) and Europe (UK, now Germany planned) we remain realistic and realise Wegovy pill on its own most likely won’t be enough to carry the whole story of a turnaround - and the market has basically showed us that already.

So, the investment thesis has become somewhat more specific. There’s no longer need for Novo to prove that people want its drugs. There’s a need to prove 3 things, in our opinion:

1.) that net pricing eventually finds a floor,

2.) that underlying margins can remain attractive as the market scales,

3.) that the company can build or acquire a credible post-semaglutide pipeline.

The first two look better than they did in February and the third looks worse.

We believe that makes the Capital Markets Day on 21 September considerably more important than another week of prescription data. Novo has shown it can still sell drugs at extraordinary scale and now it needs to show investors what comes next.

And that, more than whether Wegovy pill missed quarterly consensus by DKK 100M, will determine whether 2026 really was the trough we thought it could / would be. It will also heavily influence what we’ll do with our position - for now, we’re holding.
